item.title: Win Everything, Control No One
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
The Infinity Machine opens with a scene that has nothing to do with Demis Hassabis. In 2015, after a talk at the Royal Society, Nick Bostrom asks Geoffrey Hinton why he keeps doing AI research if he thinks political systems will use it to terrorise people. Hinton answers that he could give the usual arguments, “but the truth is that the prospect of discovery is too sweet.” Mallaby says the story haunted him, and it sets the question for the whole book: if the people building this technology understand the danger, why do they build it anyway, and does it matter what kind of people they are?

His answer is a biography of Demis Hassabis, and it is also the best account I have read of how AI got from game-playing programs to where it is now. I give it 8.5 out of 10. It is required reading for anyone who wants to understand the people behind this technology, what drives them, and why nobody seems able to stop it.

What the book is

The book does two things. It tells a life: Hassabis watching his father play chess at four and beating adults within weeks, a chess master at thirteen, a game designer at Bullfrog before university, a failed games studio, a PhD in neuroscience, DeepMind, the sale to Google, AlphaGo, AlphaFold, the Nobel Prize, and the scramble after ChatGPT. And it tells the history of the field through its ideas, in the order they arrived. Mallaby had about thirty hours with Hassabis over three years and interviewed more than a hundred people around him, so the rivals and the people who fell out with him speak in their own words.

The title comes from Cambridge. Hassabis and his friend David Silver imagined a machine that would find the patterns in a near infinity of data, and Hassabis later recruited Mustafa Suleyman with the line that an infinity machine would have infinite potential (chapters 2 and 4). Behind the phrase is the problem of induction, which symbolic AI never solved and which the rest of the book watches deep learning and reinforcement learning solve, piece by piece.

A history of AI, told in the right order

Mallaby explains the technology twice, once with an analogy and once with the mechanism. For example:

  • How an image network learns (chapter 6). The first layers find edges and patches of colour, later layers find curves and textures, deeper ones find the outline of a paw, and the last ones name the cat. Then the mechanism: weights, biases, sixty million parameters nudged until inputs match outputs.
  • Why the Atari agent needed experience replay (chapter 6). An image classifier fed a sorted stack of photos, all cats first, concludes that everything is a cat. An agent stuck in one corner of a game has the same problem. Storing experiences and sampling them at random fixed it, and Hassabis saw in it what the hippocampus does during sleep.
  • Why the Atari agent needed a second network (chapter 6). An agent that keeps adding optimism to its own estimates is like a man who finds a couple of hundred-dollar bills on the pavement and concludes he will be a billionaire by walking for a month. Mallaby’s fix is a tennis coach who watches for a while before giving advice: one network plays with frozen weights, a second one learns, and the lessons are handed over only after a period of study.
  • AlphaGo as two kinds of thinking (chapter 9). A policy network proposes moves the way a strong player sees them at a glance, a value network judges positions, and tree search does the slow deliberate part, which Mallaby maps onto Kahneman’s System One and System Two.
  • Residual networks (chapter 12). Deep networks garble their signal like a game of telephone; skip connections are express lanes past the middle layers.
  • The transformer (chapter 12). Embeddings as a map of language with hundreds of dimensions, attention as knowing which earlier episode of a crime drama you need to understand this one, and a detour through Henri Bergson on time as attention rather than sequence.

The explanations need no background and do not talk down to the reader. The order matters as much: each chapter shows what the previous breakthrough made possible and what it could not do, so the chain from ImageNet to Atari to AlphaGo to AlphaZero to the transformer to AlphaFold to reasoning models reads as one argument.

The feud at the centre

The thread that ties the history together is the rivalry between reinforcement learning and deep learning. It starts as geography: Hinton’s deep learners in Toronto, Richard Sutton’s reinforcement learners in Alberta, barely speaking. The RL theorist Csaba Szepesvári admits that neural networks work in practice but he will not use them because he cannot prove anything about them; Hinton tells his student Vlad Mnih, who wants to combine the two, “I’ve tried that. It doesn’t work.” Mnih goes to London and does it anyway, and the Atari agent is the result (chapter 6).

From there the book shows the pendulum swinging, and it never lets either side win for long:

PeriodWho looked rightWhat happenedWhat the other side contributed
2006 to 2012Deep learningHinton’s deep belief networks, then graphics chips, then Alex Krizhevsky’s ImageNet win, trained in his bedroom; his three-person company sells to Google for $44 million (chapters 4 and 6)Nothing yet: the two camps barely talk
2013Both, for the first timeDeepMind’s Atari agent learns dozens of games from pixels and a score; the room at the NIPS conference goes silent at the Breakout tunnel (chapter 6)A convolutional network to see the screen, from deep learning; Q-learning, experience replay and a second network to keep its estimates honest, from RL
2014 to 2016Reinforcement learningAlphaGo beats Fan Hui five to nothing, then Lee Sedol four to one, with Move 37 (chapter 9)The policy and value networks that stand in for intuition are deep learning, trained first on 150,000 human games
2017Reinforcement learning, loudlyAlphaZero learns Go, chess and shogi from self-play alone, with no human games at all (chapter 12)A residual network from Microsoft, deep enough to fold AlphaGo’s two networks into one
2017 to 2019Deep learningLeCun calls RL the “cherry on the cake”; the transformer and GPT learn from unlabelled text, which removes RL’s two selling points, learning without human labels and generating its own data (chapter 12)Little, until post-training
2017 to 2020Neither aloneGaia, a simulated natural world for agents, fails; AlphaStar’s win rate against StarCraft II’s built-in bots jumps from 10 to 84 percent because of a transformer, then RL takes it to 99.8 percent against ranked humans; a pure self-play StarCraft agent never gets off the ground (chapter 13)Each needed the other, and neither could do it alone
2018 to 2020Deep learning, with biologyAlphaFold starts as an RL project and wins by mostly abandoning RL; “Protein folding is not a two-player game,” Hassabis says (chapter 15)A search step in the first AlphaFold, then nothing; the decisive ideas came from evolution and the transformer
2022 to 2023Deep learning, tamed by RLChatGPT and DeepMind’s unreleased Sparrow both become usable through reinforcement learning from human feedback; Silver’s attempt to bring machine RL to Gemini stalls, because nobody can write a reward for a good haiku (chapters 16 to 18)Human raters supply the reward that the game score used to supply
2024 onwardReinforcement learning againRewards from maths and logic problems with right answers teach models to reason step by step: OpenAI’s o1, Gemini Flash Thinking, DeepSeek’s R1-Zero; AlphaProof wins an Olympiad silver medal; Silver and Sutton announce the “Era of Experience” (chapters 19 and 20)The language models being trained are deep learning; RL now runs on top of them, and so does reward hacking

Every real breakthrough in the book combines both methods, and the side that looks wrong at any moment is usually waiting for the other side’s next advance.

What DeepMind got wrong

Mallaby is a sympathetic biographer, but he does not hide DeepMind’s mistakes. DeepMind’s 2010 business plan dismissed what it called the mistaken notion that language is intelligence expressed. Hassabis believed a model had to act in the world to understand it, and he misjudged GPT for years. He admits it: “you can’t be Nostradamus every time” (chapter 13).

Afterwards he explains why. He had assumed the space of human behaviour was nearly infinite; it turned out that the roughly fourteen trillion words on the internet capture most of it. He compares the internet to the coal and oil the Industrial Revolution happened to find in the ground: nobody built it for AI, and it did not have to be there. I made the same argument from the other side in my review of Tim Berners-Lee’s memoir, The Web Was the Training Set, and Hassabis reaches it from inside the lab.

The other mistakes were organisational. Google was stuck in Xerox PARC’s dilemma: it invented the transformer and could not ship a chatbot without endangering search. DeepMind was stuck in Bell Labs’ dilemma: a culture built for open-ended exploration could not switch to engineering when the path became obvious. DeepMind had a chatbot, Sparrow, with twenty-three behavioural rules and web search, nearly ready when ChatGPT launched, and it never shipped (chapters 16 and 17).

The people

Peter Thiel backed DeepMind because it seemed contrarian and cheap, never believed in it, and nearly let it run out of money (chapter 7). Elon Musk promised money, tried to buy DeepMind for Tesla or SpaceX in a phone call from a closet, then co-founded OpenAI against it after sitting on DeepMind’s own safety board (chapters 8 and 10). Mark Zuckerberg lost DeepMind at dinner when Hassabis noticed he was just as excited about virtual reality and 3D printing as about AI, then hired Yann LeCun to poach its staff (chapter 8). Larry Page called Musk a “speciesist” for preferring humans to machines (chapter 10). Sam Altman, seen mostly through the eyes of his rivals, appears as the man who wrote in 2015 that stopping humanity from developing AI was “almost definitely not” possible, and then did more than anyone to prove it. Dario Amodei turns up as the safety researcher who scaled GPT-2 and later left to found Anthropic.

Mustafa Suleyman’s story is the hardest to read. He was the friend of Hassabis’s younger brother and became a co-founder. His health work for the NHS was good (the Streams app cut the share of unnoticed urgent kidney cases from 12.4 to 3.3 percent, chapter 11) and was killed by a tabloid story about data. His campaign to put DeepMind under independent oversight ran for three years and failed (chapter 14). Then came a bullying investigation, a sabbatical, and a Bloomberg headline, and the friendship ended. Mallaby lets both men tell their side.

Why it cannot be governed

Coming out of the book, I am more convinced than before that AI cannot be stopped, and cannot be governed, at least for now. That is my conclusion, but the book supplies most of the evidence for it. Every attempt to govern it from inside the industry fails, and the governments arrive late, with voluntary commitments:

  • The ethics and safety board Google agreed to when it bought DeepMind met once, at SpaceX. Several of its guests then founded or funded a rival lab. “Our supposed advisers were really our rivals,” Hassabis says (chapter 10).
  • The independent panel that watched over DeepMind Health was shut down when Google absorbed the health team (chapter 14).
  • Project Mario, three years of negotiation for a DeepMind with a board of three Google directors, three DeepMind directors and three independents, ended with nothing. Reid Hoffman pledged a billion dollars to a DeepMind that walked away, and it never happened (chapter 14).
  • OpenAI’s nonprofit board fired Altman and lasted five days (chapter 18).
  • The pause letter in 2023 was signed by more than a thousand people, but not by the heads of the leading labs. Hassabis’s objection holds up: a moratorium on models while chips and data centres keep improving would hand the next race to whoever has the most compute when it ends (chapter 18).

By 2025 Hassabis has concluded that “Safety isn’t about governance structures” and that the best you can do is have a seat at the table. Mallaby calls this a “flimsy scaffolding of reassurance” and admits it may be the best on offer. I agree with him on both counts.

The parts I recognised

There is a line in chapter 3 about Hassabis’s “burning desire to play and win something, anything”, which his first games studio tried to satisfy with fantasy football and StarCraft. When a colleague finally beat him at table football, he declared that his soul was on fire. I laughed, because I recognise the feeling. I played in a chess club when I was young, StarCraft is still my favourite strategy game, and I follow the Korean Brood War scene closely enough to have built a site about it. So the chapters on AlphaStar, and on AlphaGo against Lee Sedol in front of two hundred million viewers in Korea, were personal in a way most AI history is not.

So were the games. I loved Peter Molyneux’s Black & White and later Fable, and Hassabis worked on the early design of Black & White because it was the first game whose creatures changed their own rules from the player’s slaps and strokes, a small reinforcement learning system in a commercial game (chapter 2). Before that, as a teenager, he built the simulated visitors of Theme Park, who got thirsty from salty chips and sick on roller coasters. The book draws a straight line from those simulated worlds to Gaia, DeepMind’s attempt at a simulated biosphere, and to Hassabis’s fascination with Conway’s Game of Life and emergence: put simple parts together and properties appear that none of the parts had. That is the question I keep coming back to in my own simulations, from Hotaru, a simulated neuron culture that learns to play Pong, to the engines in Kishi. Kishi plays chess, shogi and Go, the same three games AlphaZero learned, and the Learning to Play series is my small-scale version of the questions in chapters 9 and 12. Hassabis also reached the top of the English shogi rankings.

The future he wants is close to the one I want: biology solved by computation, robots and automation doing the work, and abundance. He grew up on Iain Banks’s Culture novels, and in chapter 7 he goes further than most people in the industry. He doubts universal basic income is the answer and prefers what he calls universal basic provision: housing, schooling, health care and travel at a level today’s millionaires enjoy, free to every citizen, with work for anyone who wants a Ferrari. Silver, at the end of chapter 20, proposes a human right to AI assistance. Neither is a plan, but both are better starting points than most of the policy debate.

Winning without controlling

Mallaby keeps two of Hassabis’s traits in view for the whole book, and they happen to be two I share. He is ferociously competitive: Hinton calls him the only person he has met who is more competitive than Hinton. And he insists, from chapter 2 onward, that he does not want to control anyone, saying it is “really bad to manipulate or control people”, a value he traces to his mother’s church. He also does not seem to care about money. At eighteen he refused to cash a £500,000 cheque from Molyneux so he could go to Cambridge. When he sold DeepMind, he and Suleyman negotiated the research budget before the price, and in the epilogue he says he would not have swapped the Nobel for any amount of money. He drives a ten-year-old Audi and his one luxury is a Liverpool season ticket.

Mallaby tests the claim about control, and the evidence is mixed:

  • At Elixir, Hassabis’s “Jedi mind trick” inspired a team past the point of honest feedback. “Who would’ve thought that you can actually inspire people too much?” he says later (chapter 3). A psychologist tells Mallaby that charismatic people cannot avoid dominating others, however hard they try.
  • He walked away from venture capital at Elixir because giving up half the company meant being controlled. At DeepMind he took nine times as many shares as his scientific co-founder because he wanted control of the mission (chapter 5).
  • He hated domination in both directions: he would not dominate, and he would not be dominated. When Suleyman challenged his direction, he let an investigation do what a conversation should have done (chapter 14).
  • In the epilogue Mallaby puts it to him directly: “He had told me repeatedly that he didn’t want to control others. And yet he did control people.” Hassabis answers that he exercises a reluctant power, because the things he wants to do require large teams.

For anyone who likes to win and dislikes power, this is a warning: the first trait puts you in situations where you have to exercise the power the second trait wants to avoid. Hassabis’s answer, that power is acceptable as a means to the work and never as an end, is the right one. But the book shows how much discipline it takes to keep it a means.

Where it falls short

The half point I hold back is mostly about distance. Mallaby states his verdict in the introduction, that Hassabis is “decent and public-spirited”, before the evidence, and although the book does test it, Hassabis gets the last word on most disputes. OpenAI and Anthropic are seen from outside, mostly through people who left them or competed with them, so Altman is drawn almost entirely by his rivals. And Mallaby editorialises in places where he could have reported: he is hard on the independent panel that criticised DeepMind Health, generous to DeepMind in the argument over Gemini’s benchmarks, and at one point says DeepSeek’s R1-Zero was, “for all intents and purposes”, self-aware, a claim the evidence he gives does not support.

The last chapters also read like dispatches. They race through benchmarks and product names that are already dated, and they lack the calm of the chapters about Cambridge, Elixir and AlphaGo. That may be unavoidable in a book finished in 2026 about a race still running, and none of it changes my recommendation.

Who should read it

Anyone who wants to understand the last fifteen years of AI through the people who made them, with the concepts explained along the way. No technical background is needed, and if you have one, the explanations are still worth reading for their order and their analogies. It pairs well with the forecasts on my reading log such as AI 2027: those describe where this might go, and this book shows who is driving and why, and how little anyone, including the drivers, controls the route.

The book ends with Hassabis in a pub, saying that it should feel amazing to watch his dreams come true and does not, because of the mad rush. He is still optimistic.

item.title: Brain Emulation, Read as an Infrastructure Problem
item.author: Unknown
item.description:
Someone sent me an MIT thesis this week. From Worm to Human: Scaling Brain Emulation, by Isaak Freeman, submitted March 2026 in the Boyden Lab.

I read things like this fairly often. Brain emulation is nowhere near my field, but I keep more intellectual pet topics than I have time for, most of them with no obvious connection to the platform and infrastructure work that is supposedly my lane. I follow them because they are interesting, not because I can see the use up front. In my experience the payoff is almost always there. It just shows up late, and from a direction I did not predict. Connectomics has been one of them for years, a slow background read I never expected to need. Most of the time that kind of reading stays in its own compartment, a detour I do not ask to earn its keep. Every so often a detour walks straight into the problem I am actually paid to think about, and I find I have been circling the same question from two directions without noticing. This thesis was one of those times.

What pulled me in was not the biology. The abstract was doing something I have spent the last few months on this blog trying to do for software systems, just for a far more demanding workload. It was treating brain emulation as an engineering problem with identifiable bottlenecks, not a speculative aspiration defined by what we do not know.

I find that kind of reframing useful. It is what makes the difference between a research field and an engineering field. The same move that made virtual memory possible, that made hardware virtualization possible, that is currently happening to LLM serving on GPUs, was happening in this thesis to whole-brain simulation. The question stops being “is this even feasible” and starts being “what specifically is binding today, and which of those constraints sits on a known curve.”

Once you stand somewhere with that frame, the numbers do most of the work.

The shape of the claim

Freeman argues that three previously separate fronts have advanced enough that emulation of small organisms is tractable now and emulation of larger ones is on a trajectory that can be read.

The first is connectomics. For decades only the C. elegans connectome was complete, with 302 neurons. In October 2024, a team of over 200 scientists published the complete wiring diagram of an adult fruit fly brain: 139,255 neurons, 54.5 million synapses. The cost per reconstructed neuron has fallen from roughly $16,500 to about $100 for zebrafish larvae. That is not a graceful curve, that is a step change.

The second is functional imaging. The number of neurons recorded simultaneously has doubled roughly every 7.4 years. The recent ZAPBench dataset captures more than 70,000 neurons across nearly an entire larval zebrafish brain at approximately 1 Hz. Voltage imaging has reached roughly one-third of larval-zebrafish neurons.

The third is simulation. Detailed neuron and synapse models exist along a quality spectrum, from simple proxies to biologically accurate. The Allen Institute simulated nearly 10 million mouse neurons on the Fugaku supercomputer, which is the closest existing approximation to a whole-brain mammalian simulation. A Chinese team ran an 86-billion-neuron simulation on 14,012 GPUs, although Freeman is careful to note that it was too crude and oversimplified to deserve the term “emulation.”

Each of these would be a story on its own. Together they cross a threshold. Mapping, recording, and simulating are no longer in the same era they were in five years ago.

The compute math, which is what got my attention

This is the section where my idle reading turned into note-taking. The thesis stops feeling like neuroscience here and starts feeling like a substrate question.

Under what Freeman calls pessimistic assumptions, real-time human brain emulation requires roughly 6 × 1020 FLOP per second, 700 GB of memory per GPU, and 24 GB per second of interconnect bandwidth. Mid-2020s AI clusters reach roughly 4 × 1020 FLOP per second, 180 GB of memory per GPU, and 1.8 TB per second of interconnect, with larger clusters under construction.

The interesting thing in those numbers is not that the gap closes. It is the shape of the gap.

Modern AI clusters are over-provisioned on interconnect bandwidth by a factor of roughly seventy-five for this workload. They are under-provisioned on per-GPU memory by a factor of nearly four. They are slightly under-provisioned on aggregate compute. If those estimates are anywhere near right, the substrate built for LLM inference does not fit brain emulation cleanly. It overshoots on one axis, undershoots on another, and lands roughly correct on a third.

This is the same observation I have been making about the gap between LLM inference and the operating systems that schedule it. The previous time was coconutOS, where the argument was that an inference workload running on Linux is using an OS designed for human-authored sequential CPU programs. The argument generalizes. Whenever a new workload becomes economically important, the existing substrate ends up looking like an awkward fit. The fit is good enough to ship the first generation. It is not good enough to be optimal.

Brain emulation is the next test of the same principle, on a different axis. LLM inference exposed that we are running on the wrong scheduler. My bet is that brain emulation exposes the wrong memory shape.

What “the wrong memory shape” means

It is worth being concrete about why per-GPU memory is the binding constraint and interconnect is not.

A real biophysical neuron model, running with synaptic detail, needs to keep state for every synapse it touches. The fruit fly brain has 54.5 million synapses across about 140,000 neurons, which is already roughly 400 synapses per neuron on average. A human cerebral cortex has on the order of 1014 to 1015 synapses across roughly 1010 neurons. If you partition a human-scale simulation across GPUs, each GPU is responsible for some neurons and the local fraction of their synapses, plus the buffers required to integrate their activity at the simulation timestep.

Why so little interconnect, then, for so much compute? Brains are local. Most of a neuron’s synaptic targets are physically close in tissue, and the rate of cross-partition communication that has to leave a GPU and reach another GPU is bounded by the rate of neural firing across the cut. That bound is small. Spikes are sparse, the events are small, and you do not need terabit links between partitions.

You do, however, need every synapse to live somewhere fast enough to be integrated at simulation time. The simulation timestep is on the order of milliseconds. The working set has to be resident. You do not get to swap synapse state to disk the way you can swap an LLM weight tile.

So the workload looks like: many GPUs, modest per-GPU compute, very large per-GPU memory, very modest interconnect. The current AI cluster looks like: many GPUs, very high per-GPU compute, modest per-GPU memory, very high interconnect. The shape difference is real.

This is the kind of mismatch that drives architectural transitions. It is also the kind of mismatch that takes years to resolve cleanly because the existing substrate is good enough for the first wave of the new workload.

What I think this means for builders

The most interesting paragraph in Freeman’s preface is this one.

The goal throughout has been to make brain emulation legible as an engineering problem with identifiable bottlenecks, rather than a speculative aspiration defined mainly by what we do not know.

That move is what the second post of my recent trilogy, on inference-native operating systems, was trying to do. The same move sits underneath my writing on edge systems and proxy infrastructure. It is, I think, the most important shift a technical field can go through, because it changes who works in it, what their day looks like, and what the next ten years of progress look like.

If you are building infrastructure, this thesis is one more data point that the workloads coming over the horizon are not going to look like what your current scheduler, memory hierarchy, and interconnect were designed for. The gap between “the AI cluster I rent today” and “the substrate the next generation of workloads actually wants” is, I expect, going to widen rather than narrow. Brain emulation is the most extreme version of that argument I have seen so far. It is also the same argument.

A few things I would carry forward concretely.

  • I expect per-GPU memory to stay the binding constraint for an expanding class of workloads. Bandwidth is the easy axis. Density is the hard one.
  • Workloads with strong locality and large per-node state will keep showing up. They look weird on current clusters because clusters are built for the opposite shape.
  • The substrate question is durable. Every time we think the substrate is done, a workload arrives that asks a question we did not design for.

A note on the alternative-path-to-AI framing

Freeman’s thesis is also making a different argument I want to acknowledge but not centre. He places brain emulation alongside the LLM track as an alternative path to advanced AI: detailed neuronal maps of an actual human brain, replayed in simulation, as a more biologically faithful path to general intelligence than scaling transformers.

I have less to say about that framing because it pulls toward AGI-trajectory questions I have stayed off this blog. I will note only that the workload-shape argument I made above is independent of whether emulation produces something we would call intelligent. The infrastructure mismatch is real even if the simulations are only ever used for neuroscience.

The framing does sharpen one thing worth stating plainly. If emulation is a serious second path to advanced AI, then the substrate question stops being one-dimensional. Transformer scaling and brain emulation do not pull on the same hardware. Scaling transformers rewards dense compute and high interconnect bandwidth, which is precisely the cluster the industry is already building. Emulation rewards memory density and locality, which is the cluster nobody is building. Two candidate paths to a similar destination, asking for two different machines. Anyone committing capital to a single substrate roadmap today is making an implicit bet that the other path stays marginal. That bet is rarely stated out loud, and the history of computing is unkind to people who assumed the dominant workload would stay dominant.

That said, anyone reading the thesis should know the framing is in there. Freeman does not hide it. It is part of why the thesis is worth reading, even if you arrive for the engineering numbers.

I will probably come back to the thesis when the simulation and benchmarking sections give me sharper numbers than what I have used here. The State of Brain Emulation Report 2025, which Freeman cites as a multi-author companion document (arXiv:2510.15745), is also on my list. It lives at brainemulation.mxschons.com for anyone who wants the broader synthesis before I get to it.

Closing

I have spent the last few months arguing that the substrate is the next thing to bend, in proxy infrastructure, in operating systems for inference, and in the artifact engineers actually author. Brain emulation is the most demanding version of the same argument I have come across.

On Freeman’s pessimistic estimates, the AI cluster you are renting today is short by a factor of about four on per-GPU memory and about one and a half on compute: roughly a hardware generation away from running a thing nobody designed it to run. Whether the generation after that closes the gap depends on memory density growing as fast as compute has, and memory is the axis the industry is building for least, so I would not put a date on it. The question I would rather ask is what we want the substrate to look like by the time it gets there.

This is what I keep reading outside my field for. You go in for the curiosity, expecting nothing practical, and once in a while you walk out holding a sharper version of a question you already had. The brain does not care how anyone provisions a GPU. But an honest accounting of what it would take to simulate one says something true about the machines we are building for everything else, and I would not have gone looking for it on purpose.

Freeman’s thesis is the best piece of work I have read on framing that question concretely. Worth reading, even if neuroscience is not your beat.

References

  • Isaak Freeman, From Worm to Human: Scaling Brain Emulation, MIT, Boyden Lab, March 2026. The thesis this post responds to.
  • Zanichelli, Schons, Freeman, Shiu, and Arkhipov, State of Brain Emulation Report 2025 (arXiv:2510.15745). The multi-author companion synthesis, mirrored at brainemulation.mxschons.com.
  • Dorkenwald et al., Neuronal wiring diagram of an adult brain, Nature 634, 124-138 (2024). The FlyWire adult Drosophila connectome: 139,255 neurons, ~5 × 107 synapses.
  • Immer et al., ZAPBench: A Benchmark for Whole-Brain Activity Prediction in Zebrafish, ICLR 2025. Light-sheet recording of more than 70,000 neurons across a larval zebrafish brain.
  • Allen Institute, One of the world’s most detailed virtual brain simulations (2025). Roughly 10 million mouse-cortex neurons and 26 billion synapses simulated on Fugaku, presented at SC25.
  • Lu et al., Simulation and assimilation of the digital human brain, Nature Computational Science (2024). The 86-billion-neuron, 47.8-trillion-synapse spiking simulation on 14,012 GPUs.
